statement: Hiragana and katakana both derive from man'yōgana (Chinese characters used phonetically for Japanese sounds, traceable to the 5th century CE); hiragana emerged as cursive simplification of whole man'yōgana kanji, katakana by taking fragments/components of kanji, both taking recognizable shape in the 9th-century Heian period. The popular attribution of hiragana's invention to the monk Kūkai (774-835 CE) is a legend, not documented history: no signed document supports it, and modern scholarship has similarly revised the traditional Kūkai attribution for the Iroha poem to a later Heian-period date. The documented picture instead shows a gradual, collective, multi-decade development with no single named inventor.
